title: Mean Value on Each Tree Level
statement:
You get the root of a non-empty binary tree. The root is on level 0, its children on level 1, and so on.

Return a list with the average of the node values on each level, from the top level down. Averages are real numbers; answers within 10⁻⁵ of the exact value are accepted.

examples.why: Level 1 holds 2 and 9, averaging 5.5, not 5: keep the fraction. Level 2 holds 1, 4 and 8: 13 / 3.
Negative values average the same way.
A chain has one node per level, so each average is just that node.

hints: You need to group nodes by level. Which traversal naturally visits one level at a time?
Breadth-first search with a queue. At the start of each round the queue holds exactly one level; its length tells you how many nodes to take out.
For each round, add up the values of that many nodes (pushing their children), then divide by the count. A depth-first walk with per-depth sum and count arrays also works.

explain.intuition:
Averages per level need two numbers per level: the sum and the count. A breadth-first walk processed in rounds gives both directly. When a round starts, the queue contains exactly the current level, so record its size, pop that many nodes while summing their values and pushing their children, and divide.

A depth-first walk works as well if you pass the depth along: keep sum[depth] and count[depth], and divide at the end. That is the same idea as walking a nested DOM tree and collecting statistics per nesting depth. Either way, divide as a real number. Languages with fixed-width integers also need a 64-bit sum, since a level can hold thousands of values near 2³¹.
steps: Put the root in a queue.
While the queue is not empty: let size be its length and sum = 0.
Pop size nodes. Add each value to sum and push its non-null children.
pitfalls: Integer division. Level 1 of the first example averages 5.5, not 5.
Reading the queue length inside the loop while children are being pushed, which mixes two levels into one round.
In Java or C++, summing into a 32-bit integer. Three values of 2³¹ − 1 overflow it.

complexity.space: O(w) for the queue, where w is the widest level

solutions.title: Depth-first with per-level totals
solutions.idea: Walk the tree with the depth as a parameter, collecting a sum and a count for each depth, then divide.
solutions.space: O(h) for the recursion plus O(levels)

solutions.title: Breadth-first in rounds
solutions.idea: Each round of the queue is one level. Sum that round and divide by its size.

followups: Return the median of each level instead of the mean. What extra work does that need?
The tree is very deep (a chain of 100 000 nodes). Which of the two solutions is safer in JavaScript, and why?
